title: Refactoring Techniques
tagline: Improve code structure without changing observable behaviour — detect smells, apply named refactorings, and keep the test suite green the entire time.

sections.content:
Every senior engineer has stared at a function that is 300 lines long, has six nested `if` statements, uses variables named `x`, `tmp`, and `data2`, and returns seven different things depending on a magic number buried on line 247. The function works — the tests pass, users are happy — but nobody in the team wants to touch it. That paralysis is the quiet cost of poor code structure, and it compounds over time.

**Refactoring** is the disciplined practice of improving a codebase's internal structure without changing its external, observable behaviour. It is not a rewrite, and it is not a cleanup sprint you schedule once a year. It is a continuous, micro-scale activity woven into daily development: a deliberate sequence of small, named, behaviour-preserving transformations, each verified by an automated test suite.

The concept was systematised by Martin Fowler in *Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code* (1999, revised 2018), a catalogue of more than 60 named refactorings that gave the engineering community a shared vocabulary. Before Fowler's book, developers would say 'I cleaned up the code a bit.' After it, they could say 'I applied Extract Function, Introduce Parameter Object, and Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.' That precision matters: named techniques can be taught, reviewed, debated, and safely applied by any team member.

The workflow is deceptively simple: **red → green → refactor**. First, ensure the current behaviour is covered by a test. Then make the smallest meaningful structural improvement. Then run the tests to confirm nothing broke. Commit. Repeat. This rhythm is how large, frightening legacy codebases are safely and sustainably improved — not in one heroic all-nighter, but one micro-step at a time over weeks and months. Understanding refactoring deeply is one of the highest-leverage skills a working engineer can develop, because it is the mechanism by which good design is maintained in the presence of real-world change.

sections.caption: Refactoring is a tight, repeating loop: detect a smell, confirm test coverage, apply a named transformation, verify tests stay green, then commit. Each cycle should take minutes, not hours.

sections.title: Renovating a House Without Evicting the Tenants
sections.content:
Refactoring is like renovating a house while the tenants are still living in it — every door and every light switch must keep working throughout. You can repaint a room (**Rename Variable**), move a non-structural wall (**Extract Function**), rewire an outlet (**change a data structure**), or knock two small rooms into one large one (**Inline Function**). But if you accidentally seal a door while rearranging, the tenant notices immediately and you have to undo the change before you continue.

The **automated tests are the tenants**. If any test fails, a door is broken. You must fix it — or undo the transformation — before proceeding. This constraint is what makes refactoring safe rather than risky. Without tests, what looks like 'cleaning up the code' is actually editing with hope, and that is how hard-to-trace regressions get introduced.

A **code smell** is the equivalent of noticing the kitchen is overcrowded, a corridor is oddly narrow, and three rooms share a single socket. None of these are structural failures — the house is standing, the tenants are alive — but they are signals that the layout accumulated piecemeal over time and needs deliberate attention. Smells are not crimes; they are opportunities. The question is not 'Is this code wrong?' but 'Is this code as clear and as easy to change as it could be?' Refactoring is the answer.

sections.title: Code Smells: The Warning Signs
sections.content:
A **code smell** is a surface-level symptom that suggests — but does not guarantee — an underlying design problem worth investigating. Fowler and Kent Beck catalogued dozens of them. The most common ones you will encounter in real codebases are:

**Long Method**: A function longer than about 20 lines is almost always doing more than one thing. The cognitive overhead of reading it is high because a reader must hold the entire function's context in mind simultaneously. The fix is **Extract Function**: pull a coherent block of code into a new, well-named function. Short functions are not always better, but if a function needs a comment to explain what each section does, those sections are begging to be named functions.

**Duplicate Code**: The same logic appears in two or more places. When a bug is fixed in one copy, the other copy silently retains the bug. The fix is to extract the shared logic into a single shared function or method and reference it from both call sites. DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself — exists precisely to avoid this drift.

**Large Class**: A class accumulates responsibilities over time until it has dozens of methods and hundreds of lines. The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change; a Large Class typically has five. The fix is to split it into focused, cohesive sub-classes.

**Long Parameter List**: More than three or four parameters makes a function hard to call, hard to read, and hard to extend. If you add a fifth parameter, you must update every call site. The fix is **Introduce Parameter Object**: group related parameters into a plain object or data class.

**Magic Numbers and Strings**: Literal values like `0.1`, `1000`, `'premium'`, or `86400` scattered throughout code are opaque. The reader has no idea what they represent without studying context. The fix is **Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant**: `const SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400`.

**Dead Code**: Unreachable branches, commented-out blocks, unused variables, and functions that are never called. Dead code creates cognitive noise and creates a false impression that it might matter. Delete it without mercy — version control remembers it.

**Feature Envy**: A method that reaches into another class's data far more than it uses its own class's data is envious of that other class. The fix is **Move Function**: relocate the method to the class whose data it uses. The method and the data it depends on should live together.

**Comments as Deodorant**: A comment that explains *what* code does (rather than *why* a non-obvious decision was made) is a sign the code should explain itself. 'Calculate the discount' as a comment above a block of arithmetic is a missed opportunity to use Extract Function and name the extracted function `calculateDiscount`. Comments on *why* — business rules, legal constraints, non-obvious performance optimisations — remain valuable and should be preserved.

sections.title: The Core Named Refactorings
sections.content:
Named refactorings are the vocabulary of structural improvement. Using them precisely in code reviews and pull request descriptions helps teammates understand not just what changed, but why and how it was done safely.

**Extract Function** is the most frequently applied refactoring. You take a fragment of code — perhaps four lines that calculate a sub-result — and move it into a new function with a name that communicates its purpose. You then replace the original fragment with a call to the new function. The inverse, **Inline Function**, is used when a function's body is as clear as the function's name, and the indirection is adding no value.

**Rename Variable / Function / Class** is arguably the most *important* refactoring. A well-chosen name is the most powerful form of documentation because it is always in sync with the code. Renaming `x` to `monthlyInterestRate`, or `process` to `applyPremiumDiscount`, instantly makes the surrounding code more readable. Modern IDEs make this safe — they find every reference automatically.

**Introduce Parameter Object** groups a cluster of related parameters into a single cohesive object. `createOrder(customerId, productId, qty, discountCode, shippingType)` becomes `createOrder(orderDetails)` where `orderDetails` is a plain object. The call site becomes self-documenting because parameter names are now key names, and adding a sixth option requires no signature change.

**Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant** moves a literal value to a named constant at the top of the module. The value is now documented, lives in one place, and changes to it propagate automatically.

**Extract Variable** (also called Explaining Variable) gives a complex expression a meaningful name. A long boolean condition like `user.age >= 18 && !user.banned && account.tier === 'premium'` becomes `const isEligibleForDiscount = ...`. The `if` statement that follows now reads like English.

**Move Function** relocates a function to the module or class where it logically belongs, fixing Feature Envy. If `calculateCustomerDiscount` lives in `OrderService` but only ever touches `Customer` data, it belongs in `CustomerService` or the `Customer` class itself.

**Decompose Conditional** extracts complex `if/else` conditions and branches into well-named helper functions. The `if` becomes `if (isEligibleForExpressShipping(order))` instead of an inline compound boolean expression.

**Replace Conditional with Polymorphism** (or its simpler JavaScript variant, the strategy map / lookup table) swaps a long `switch` or chained `if/else if` that dispatches on type. Instead of adding a new `else if` branch every time a new type appears, you add a new entry to a dispatch table or a new subclass. The core function never changes.

**Encapsulate Field** converts a public data field into a private field accessed only via getter/setter methods. This is the gateway to adding validation, logging, change notifications, or derived fields in a single location. Without encapsulation, every direct write to the field must be found and updated individually.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Notice that every `console.log` produces the same result before and after — that is the definition of refactoring. The function name changed from the opaque `process` to the precise `calcFinalBalance`. The single-letter parameters became `user` and `tierType`. The magic numbers became named constants. And two sub-responsibilities (eligibility check, discount calculation) became their own named functions. The total code is slightly longer but vastly more readable and testable: `isEligibleForDiscount` and `calcDiscount` can now be unit-tested independently.

sections.title: Replace Conditional with Strategy: Eliminating Type-Checking Chains
sections.content:
One of the most impactful structural improvements you can make is eliminating chains of `if/else if` or `switch` statements that dispatch on a type or category. These chains have a characteristic failure mode: every time a new type is added, a developer must remember to add a new branch in *every* place where the dispatch occurs. Miss one, and you have a silent bug.

The **strategy pattern** — represented in JavaScript as a simple object map — fixes this. You define a data structure that maps each type name to its handler. To add a new type, you add one entry to the map. The dispatch function itself never changes.

This is a simplified version of the **Replace Conditional with Polymorphism** refactoring. In a class-based system, each type would be a subclass overriding a polymorphic method. In functional JavaScript, the strategy map achieves the same result without the overhead of a class hierarchy.

The pattern also makes the structure visible as data, which means it can be inspected, iterated, and tested independently. You can write a test that asserts every key in the strategy map produces a valid result, without knowing the specific types in advance.

This refactoring is especially valuable when you see the same `switch` statement duplicated in multiple places — often a `switch` for rendering, another for validation, another for pricing, all switching on the same type. Each duplication is a future maintenance trap. The fix is to unify all type-specific behaviour into one location — either a class hierarchy or a registry — and have each branch handle all its own concerns.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The strategy map co-locates all the properties of each type in one place. Before, adding 'overnight' required editing two functions — and in a real codebase there might be five or ten such switch-on-type functions scattered across services, validators, and renderers. The strategy map reduces that to one edit and zero missed cases. The `??` (nullish coalescing) operator provides the default, replacing the final fallthrough in the original if-chain.

sections.title: Introduce Parameter Object and Encapsulate Field
sections.content:
Two refactorings that significantly improve long-term code health are often overlooked because they feel like ceremony at first glance.

**Introduce Parameter Object** addresses the **Long Parameter List** smell. When a function grows and needs to accept additional configuration, the natural impulse is to add another parameter. After five or six additions, you have a function signature that is nearly impossible to call correctly from memory, and positional argument order bugs become common. Grouping related parameters into a plain object (or a dedicated class) solves this: the keys are self-documenting, order is irrelevant, and adding a seventh option requires no change to the function signature — only the destructuring pattern inside the function and the call sites that actually need the new option.

**Encapsulate Field** is one of the most powerful refactorings for long-term correctness. When a class exposes a data field as a public property, every piece of code in the system can write to it directly. This is fine initially. But the moment you need to add validation — reject negative balances, clamp a value to a range, fire an event when a status changes — you face an impossible search problem: find every direct assignment in the entire codebase and update it. Encapsulate Field moves access through getter and setter methods, creating a single chokepoint. Validation logic lives in the setter. Logging, change tracking, or event dispatch can be added to that one location without touching any call site.

Private class fields in modern JavaScript (using the `#` prefix) enforce encapsulation at the language level — a direct assignment from outside the class is a syntax error, so the compiler enforces the pattern rather than relying on developer discipline.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The parameter object pattern is especially valuable in APIs that will evolve: you can add optional fields without breaking existing call sites. Extract Variable is arguably underused — naming a complex condition is one of the fastest ways to make code review easier. And Encapsulate Field illustrates a key principle: structural refactoring pays forward. The `deposit` and `withdraw` methods both reuse the setter's validation for free — any future rule change to what constitutes a valid balance needs to be made in exactly one place.

sections.caption: Encapsulate Field transforms a public mutable property into a private field with a controlled access point. Any rule about valid values — minimum, maximum, type check, event emission — is added to the setter once and applies everywhere.

sections.title: The Test Safety Net: Why Tests Are Non-Negotiable
sections.content:
Refactoring and automated testing are inseparable. The definition of refactoring — behaviour-preserving transformation — is meaningless without a mechanism to verify that behaviour was indeed preserved. The test suite is that mechanism.

Every named refactoring is designed to be applied in a way that cannot logically change observable behaviour. Renaming a variable, extracting a block of code into a named function, grouping parameters into an object — none of these change what the function returns for any given input. But humans make mistakes. An extract might accidentally capture the wrong variable. A rename might introduce a shadowing conflict. A move might not update all call sites.

Tests catch these mistakes within seconds of introducing them, while the change is fresh in mind and trivial to undo. Without tests, a mistake might be discovered days or weeks later, when many subsequent changes have piled on top of it and tracing the root cause is a detective story.

The practical implication is: **if code is not covered by a test, you should write a characterisation test before refactoring it**. A characterisation test does not assert that the code does what the spec says it should; it asserts that the code does what the code currently does. This preserves existing (possibly buggy) behaviour through the structural change. Once the refactoring is complete, you can then separately fix bugs if needed — but that is a separate commit.

**Testing granularity** also matters. Coarse integration tests tell you that the system as a whole is not broken, but they do not pinpoint which extracted function has the wrong logic. Fine-grained unit tests on individual functions let you identify a failure in seconds. After refactoring creates new named functions (`isEligibleForDiscount`, `calcDiscount`), those functions should get their own unit tests. The refactoring made them testable; the tests make subsequent changes to them safe.

**IDE support** accelerates safe refactoring significantly. Modern IDEs (VS Code with TypeScript, IntelliJ, PyCharm) perform rename refactorings across an entire codebase atomically — finding every reference, including in template strings, comments, and import statements. Using the IDE's refactoring tools rather than find-and-replace reduces the risk of a missed reference. But IDE tools are a convenience, not a substitute for tests: the IDE cannot tell you whether the logic is correct after transformation.

sections.title: When to Refactor and When to Stop
sections.content:
One of the most practically useful questions is not *how* to refactor but *when* — and, equally important, *when to stop*.

**The Boy Scout Rule**: Leave the code slightly cleaner than you found it. Every time you open a file to add a feature or fix a bug, spend five minutes on a small improvement in the area you are already touching. Rename one unclear variable. Extract one long expression. This is how codebases improve without dedicated 'cleanup sprints', because cleanup happens continuously as a side-effect of normal development.

**The Rule of Three**: The first time you see something done one way, just do it. The second time, notice the similarity. The third time, refactor. This heuristic prevents premature abstraction (generalising code before you understand the actual variation points) while reliably catching real duplication.

**Refactor before adding a feature**: If the code structure makes the new feature hard to add, first refactor it into a shape where the feature becomes easy, then add the feature. This is Kent Beck's famous two-hats metaphor: wear the 'refactoring hat' first (behaviour preserved), then switch to the 'feature hat' (behaviour changed). Never wear both hats simultaneously.

**When to stop**: Refactoring is subject to diminishing returns. A function that was 300 lines is much better at 50 lines; whether squeezing it to 30 lines provides additional value depends on context. Stop when the code is clear enough that a new team member could understand it without asking questions, when the area you are working in no longer causes friction, and when the test suite runs green. Over-refactoring — excessive indirection, too many tiny functions with names that are more confusing than the code they replaced, or premature abstraction — is a real failure mode that makes code harder, not easier, to understand.

**Large-scale refactoring** — changing an architecture, splitting a module, migrating a data structure — follows the same principles but requires more planning. The key technique is the **strangler fig pattern**: build the new structure alongside the old one, gradually redirect calls from old to new, then delete the old. This keeps the system working at all times. Never attempt a big-bang replacement of a critical module in one commit.

sections.title: Refactoring in Practice: Tooling, Workflow, and Team Culture
sections.content:
Refactoring alone is necessary but not sufficient — the surrounding workflow and team culture determine whether it actually happens and whether it stays safe.

**Separate commits** are the most important workflow discipline. A commit that does only refactoring should say so clearly: `refactor: extract isEligibleForDiscount from calcFinalBalance`. A commit that adds a feature says: `feat: add premium discount calculation`. When a bug appears, `git bisect` can pinpoint the exact commit that changed behaviour. If refactoring and feature work are mixed, bisect shows you commits that changed structure and behaviour simultaneously, making root cause analysis far harder.

**Static analysis tools** (ESLint with complexity rules, SonarQube, language-specific linters) can automatically flag code smells: cyclomatic complexity above a threshold, functions longer than N lines, parameters lists longer than M items. Integrating these into CI makes the team aware of new smells as they are introduced, preventing the codebase from drifting back toward the messy state you started from.

**Refactoring vocabulary in code review** is a force multiplier. When a reviewer says 'Consider Introduce Parameter Object here,' the author knows exactly what to do. When a reviewer says 'This smells like Feature Envy,' the author knows where to look for the problem. A team that shares this vocabulary can give and receive precise, actionable feedback in code reviews, making the review process faster and more valuable.

**Technical debt** is the metaphor for the accumulated cost of poor structural decisions. Like financial debt, small amounts are manageable and sometimes the right trade-off (move fast now, pay it back later). But unchecked technical debt compounds: messy code makes the next change slower, which makes the next sprint shorter, which creates pressure to cut corners, which creates more mess. Refactoring is the debt payment — and, like financial debt, the earlier you pay it, the less total interest you pay.

sections.content: **Historical context:** The word 'refactoring' was used informally among Smalltalk programmers in the late 1980s. Bill Opdyke formalised it in his 1992 PhD thesis, describing behaviour-preserving program transformations. John Brant and Don Roberts built the first automated refactoring browser for Smalltalk in 1997. Martin Fowler and Kent Beck collaborated on *Refactoring* (1999), which made the practice and its vocabulary mainstream across all languages. The book's second edition (2018) rewrote all examples in JavaScript, reflecting the language's dominance in modern development. IDE support for automated refactoring (Eclipse's 2001 Java refactoring tools were pioneering) removed most of the mechanical risk, making refactoring a routine part of development rather than a special occasion.

**Interview and practical traps to know cold:**

- 'Refactoring does not change behaviour' — if an interviewer asks you to refactor code and you change what it returns, that is a bug, not a refactoring.
- 'You need tests before refactoring' — if asked how to safely refactor untested legacy code, the correct first step is to write characterisation tests, not to start restructuring blindly.
- 'Never refactor and add features in the same commit' — a classic process question in system design and engineering leadership interviews.
- 'Comments that explain what code does are a smell' — they should be replaced with Extract Function and better naming; comments explaining why (business rules, trade-offs) are valuable and should stay.
- 'The Rule of Three for duplication' — don't abstract on the first or second occurrence; wait for the third to understand the real commonality.
- 'Strangler fig for large-scale refactoring' — named after the vine that gradually replaces a host tree; build alongside, redirect, delete. Never big-bang replace.

items: **Refactoring** is behaviour-preserving restructuring — the external contract stays identical, only the internal structure improves. If you change what a function returns, that is a bug fix or feature addition, not a refactoring.

**Code smells** — Long Method, Duplicate Code, Magic Numbers, Feature Envy, Long Parameter List, Large Class, Dead Code, Comments as Deodorant — are signals that point toward structural improvements, not crimes that require immediate emergency surgery.

**Named refactorings** (Extract Function, Rename, Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant, Extract Variable, Move Function, Decompose Conditional, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Encapsulate Field) provide a shared vocabulary so teams can discuss structural changes precisely and quickly.

**Tests are the safety net** — never refactor code that has no automated test coverage. Write characterisation tests first if needed, run the suite after every micro-step, and treat a red test as an immediate signal to undo the last change.

**Commit refactoring and feature work separately** — one commit that is purely structural, one that adds behaviour. This discipline makes `git bisect`, `git blame`, and code review dramatically more effective and keeps each change individually revertable.

**Two hats, two timelines** — when a code structure makes a feature hard to add, put on the refactoring hat first (improve structure, keep behaviour), then switch to the feature hat (add behaviour). Never wear both simultaneously.

**Refactoring is continuous, not periodic** — the Boy Scout Rule (leave code slightly cleaner than you found it) and the Rule of Three (abstract on the third occurrence, not the first) turn refactoring from a special cleanup event into a sustainable daily habit that prevents technical debt from compounding.

quiz.question: What is the defining constraint that separates refactoring from other code changes?
options: You must add at least one new unit test per refactoring session
The external observable behaviour must remain unchanged
You must use an IDE refactoring tool — manual edits do not count
Each refactoring must reduce the line count of the file
quiz.explanation: Refactoring is specifically defined as improving internal structure WITHOUT changing external behaviour. If the return values or side-effects of any function change, the transformation is a bug fix or a feature addition — not a refactoring.

quiz.question: Which refactoring technique is applied when you move a block of code into its own separately-named function?
options: Rename Variable
Introduce Parameter Object
Extract Function
Encapsulate Field
quiz.explanation: Extract Function takes a code fragment and moves it into a new function whose name communicates its purpose. It is the most frequently applied refactoring and the primary fix for the Long Method smell. Its inverse is Inline Function.

quiz.question: A function uses `0.1` and `86400` as unexplained literals throughout its body. Which refactoring should you apply?
options: Extract Function
Decompose Conditional
Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant
Move Function
quiz.explanation: Magic numbers are a code smell because they are opaque — a reader cannot understand their intent without studying context. Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant extracts each literal into a named constant (e.g. `const SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400`), so the intent is explicit and the value lives in exactly one place.

quiz.question: A method in `ReportService` accesses and manipulates data from `Customer` objects far more than it uses any `ReportService` data. What code smell does this indicate and what is the prescribed fix?
options: Dead Code — the method is unused and should be deleted
Feature Envy — move the method to `Customer` where its data lives (Move Function)
Long Parameter List — introduce a Parameter Object
Large Class — split `ReportService` into multiple focused classes
quiz.explanation: Feature Envy occurs when a method is more interested in another class's data than in its own class's data. The fix is Move Function — relocate the method to the class whose data it depends on. This aligns behaviour with the data it operates on, a fundamental cohesion principle.

quiz.question: You replace a chain of `if (type === 'express') ... else if (type === 'standard')...` checks with a lookup object `{ express: 25, standard: 10, free: 0 }`. Which refactoring is this closest to?
options: Introduce Parameter Object
Extract Variable
Encapsulate Field
Replace Conditional with Polymorphism / Strategy
quiz.explanation: Replacing a type-checking conditional chain with a strategy map (or a polymorphic dispatch via subclasses) is the Replace Conditional with Polymorphism refactoring. It makes adding a new type a data change rather than a logic change, and eliminates the risk of forgetting to update one of several duplicated switch statements.

quiz.question: What should be the FIRST step before refactoring a legacy function that has no automated test coverage?
options: Immediately begin applying Extract Function to reduce line count
Ask a senior engineer to approve the refactoring plan
Write characterisation tests that capture the function's current behaviour
Delete the function and rewrite it from scratch
quiz.explanation: Without tests, refactoring is editing with hope. A characterisation test does not assert what the spec says the function should do — it asserts what the function actually does right now. This creates a safety net that will immediately catch any accidental behaviour change during the subsequent structural work.

quiz.question: Why should refactoring commits be kept strictly separate from feature-addition commits?
options: Git cannot handle both types of change in the same commit
Mixing them makes it impossible to isolate which commit introduced a behaviour change or bug using git bisect
Refactoring commits must be tagged with a version bump by the CI system
IDEs require separate commits for refactoring to update their symbol indexes
quiz.explanation: When a bug appears, `git bisect` and `git blame` are far more effective if every commit is either a pure structural change (no behaviour change) or a pure behaviour change. Mixing them makes causality impossible to trace automatically and forces slow manual investigation.

quiz.question: What does the 'Rule of Three' heuristic say about when to extract duplicated code into a shared abstraction?
options: Abstract immediately after writing the same logic twice
Abstract when the same logic appears for the third time
Never abstract — duplication is always preferable to abstraction
Abstract only when the duplicated logic exceeds 10 lines
quiz.explanation: The Rule of Three advises: do it once and move on; the second time notice it; the third time refactor. Abstracting after the first or second occurrence risks premature generalisation — you may not yet understand the real variation points. Waiting for the third occurrence gives you enough examples to see the actual commonality.

quiz.question: Encapsulate Field replaces direct public field access with getter and setter methods. What is the primary long-term benefit of this refactoring?
options: It makes the field invisible to unit tests, improving test isolation
It reduces memory usage by removing the field from the object
It creates a single chokepoint where validation, logging, or change notifications can be added without modifying every call site
It automatically generates API documentation for the field
quiz.explanation: Once all access is channelled through a setter, you can add validation (reject invalid values), logging, or event emission in one place. Without encapsulation, every direct write to the field must be found and updated individually across the entire codebase — an error-prone and time-consuming process.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the 'strangler fig' pattern and when it is used?
options: A pattern for removing dead code by deleting the entire module and rewriting it
A pattern for large-scale refactoring: build the new structure alongside the old, gradually redirect calls, then delete the old — keeping the system working throughout
A pattern for replacing magic numbers with constants one file at a time
A design pattern for implementing the Observer interface in event-driven systems
quiz.explanation: The strangler fig pattern (named after the vine that gradually replaces its host tree) is the safe approach to large-scale architectural refactoring. It avoids big-bang replacements by building new and old implementations side by side, migrating callers incrementally, and only deleting the old implementation once all traffic has been redirected and verified.
